lesson.title: Kitchen & Book Set
lesson.subtitle: Küche, Buch, Milch, suchen, sprechen — and the seek/beseech proof

hook.title: English Did It Too — Twice
hook.content: English will swear it never softened a k into a ch. Then you catch it in the act — inside its own noun-verb pairs. Seek became beseech (and German says suchen). Speak became speech (and German says sprechen). English performed the velar shift exactly once per pair, keeping the k-version as the everyday verb and the ch-version as the fancy one. German performed it everywhere: Küche (kitchen), Buch (book), Milch (milk), Koch (cook). Your kitchen is a museum of both outcomes.

footnotes.title: Kirk and Kirche
footnotes.content: Both English kirk (still the word for 'church' in Scotland) and German Kirche descend from Greek kyriakon ('the Lord's house'). Scottish English kept the k; German melted it to ch — the same word on two sides of one shift.

pattern.title: The Household CH Set
pattern.content: cook → kochen, kitchen → Küche, book → Buch, milk → Milch, week → Woche, seek → suchen, speak → sprechen, break → brechen. The vowel compass still steers the sound: after back vowels the throat growls (kochen, Buch, Woche — Ach-Laut), after front vowels and l it whispers (Küche, Milch, sprechen — Ich-Laut). English even kept the whisper: the ch of speech and beseech is the same soft sound German writes in sprechen and suchen.
pattern.linguist_note: Buch and book both lengthened their vowel and lost the k in German only: book's k stayed because English never ran the shift; Buch's k became the Ach-Laut [x] after the back vowel u.

exercises.prompt: Match the household words through the K → CH lens:
exercises.target_answer: Milch, Buch, suchen, sprechen, Knochen, riechen, Koch
exercises.meaning: milk, book, to seek, to speak, bone, to smell, cook
exercises.explanation: English softened the k in beseech and speech; German softened it in every one of these words — the cook's own title, Koch, wears the shift on its face.

options: The vowel decides: back vowel u → Ach-Laut, front vowel i → Ich-Laut
exercises.target_answer: The vowel decides: back vowel u → Ach-Laut, front vowel i → Ich-Laut
exercises.meaning: The vowel compass of the German ch
exercises.explanation: a, o, u pull the tongue back (Buch, kochen, Woche); e, i, ä, ö, ü and l/r whisper forward (Milch, sprechen, Küche) — weich whispers too: k went soft, and the word for soft went with it.
week → Woche: k softened to ch after the back vowel o (with the usual vowel alignment).

exercises.prompt: What English verb pair proves English also ran k → ch — seek became...?
exercises.explanation: seek/beseech is English's own k→ch pair — and beseech's vowel matches suchen exactly.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "The tongue finds the cake sweet"
exercises.target_answer: Die Zunge findet den Kuchen süß
exercises.meaning: The tongue finds the cake sweet

vocab_hints.note: der Kuchen becomes den Kuchen when it is what's found — the him-case you will meet properly soon

exercises.explanation: finden takes the object straight on: die Zunge findet den Kuchen süß — the tongue renders its verdict, and every ch in the kitchen whispers.
exercises.idea: The tongue finds the cake sweet
cues: Start with "Die" and anchor "Zunge" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Use the household CH set in a real sentence and steer Ach- vs Ich-Laut by vowel.

use_example.german: Die Zunge findet den Kuchen süß.
use_example.english: The tongue finds the cake sweet.

summary.takeaway: Küche, Buch, Milch, suchen, sprechen — the kitchen set proves the velar shift, and English's seek/beseech proves English ran it too.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: K→CH discrimination — predict the ch-sound of unseen words and catch the k-impostors.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Kitchen & Book Set (The tongue finds the cake sweet):
twist.target_answer: Die Zunge findet den Kuchen süß
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Die Zunge findet den Kuchen süß" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Kitchen & Book Set without relying on short-term echo.

küche.context_translation: We are cooking in the kitchen.

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

suchen.context_translation: I am looking for my glasses.
suchen.etymology_derivation: k → ch. Direct transitive object without prepositions.

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

knochen.context_phrase: Der Hund kaut an einem Knochen.
knochen.context_translation: The dog is chewing on a bone.
knochen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *knokō 'bone, joint' — cognate with English knuckle; German k shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

riechen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German riohhan, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. English reek is a listed cognate, keeping the k where German shifted to ch. [wiktionary]

koch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kok — a true k → ch shift word (cook ↔ Koch). [wiktionary]

süß.context_phrase: Der Kuchen ist zu süß für mich.
süß.context_translation: The cake is too sweet for me.
süß.etymology_derivation: süß — from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, PIE *swéh₂dus, exactly cognate with English sweet; the final t shifted to ß and the old w was lost before the rounded vowel. [wiktionary]

welch.etymology_derivation: k → ch (Old English hwelc ↔ German welch).

mittwoch.etymology_derivation: Mitte + Woche — literally mid-week; the entry cites English midweek as the cognate compound and notes it calqued Latin media hebdomas. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
